output.title: Why some errors keep coming back
output.body:
Self-reinforcing errors survive when a repeated workflow has no built-in check. The error is not mysterious; it keeps getting reintroduced because the loop only tells you something went wrong after the damage has already moved downstream. In a small business, that often shows up in order entry, invoice handling, customer-data updates, or lead follow-up: the same mistake repeats because nobody sees it at the point where it can still be stopped.

The practical question is simple: where does the workflow first produce a measurable output, and who reviews it? If the answer is “later in the week” or “only after a customer complains,” the feedback loop is too slow. If the answer is “nobody,” the loop is open.

The next step is to add one bounded control at that exact point: a single human approval gate, a weekly review, or a basic validation rule such as duplicate detection or amount checking. Keep money movement and other high-risk decisions human-approved. AI can help route or flag issues, but it should not be trusted to approve the risky part. That is usually where the tidy error gets its second life. The fix is less glamorous than a grand redesign, which is inconvenient but useful.

If the workflow is frequent, rule-based, and still mostly manual, start there: one check, one owner, one review point before the mistake reaches a customer or the bank.
